author: @PattonAnalytics
title_or_hook: Putting Yourself in a Hole: expected-pass situations are mostly game script (thread, part 1)
summary: A method audit of the popular QB efficiency in obvious passing situations chart, read in full at the author's Substack. Definitions: expected pass rate (xpass) per play from down, distance, field position, score, and time. Findings from every regular-season snap 2016-2026: the right bucket edges are 40% and 75% xpass (efficiency flat near +0.10 EPA/dropback into the low 70s, +0.049 at 75-94%, roughly zero above 94%; a 300-resample bootstrap put the break between 74% and 76% about eight times in ten); expected-pass dropbacks average +0.026 EPA vs +0.097 neutral; the headline correlation (-0.56 all seasons, -0.63 in 2026) is mostly the scoreboard (removing win-probability-under-20% dropbacks cuts it to -0.37, and about 91% of the first-half effect runs through the halftime score); expected-pass RATE is a team/scoreboard property (year-to-year stickiness 0.45 for QBs who stay, 0.13 for the 63 who changed teams) while EPA in those spots travels with the QB (0.32 stay / 0.30 move); a residual of about -0.3 survives every script control. Numbers CITED from a full source read, not yet reproduced in-house.
metrics_or_datasets: xpass bucket EPA means (neutral, 75-94%, 94%+)
Correlation of expected-pass share vs efficiency, raw and WP-filtered
QB stickiness of expected-pass rate vs EPA in expected-pass spots
engine_training_value: Direct: xpass bucket + WP band become features; first-half neutral EPA is a label-bearing predictor of second-half script load. The dataset is nflverse play-by-play GSE already holds; labels are in the plays themselves.
provenance: The poster (@PattonAnalytics) is the method author; article read in full at source this run. The chart family it audits is the weekly Hoppen/ghatz_28 obvious-passing-situations chart; xpass is the standard nflverse-model family (nflfastR xpass).

title_or_hook: "Walking" the Will: Nickel that becomes Penny without substituting (text-complete; diagram chart-locked)

title_or_hook: Adaptive k-NN from the local shape operator (arXiv:2409.05084)
summary: A classification method (kK-NN): instead of a fixed neighbor count k, each point's neighborhood size adapts to its local curvature, estimated from the local shape operator (built from the local covariance and Hessian). Low-curvature regions get larger neighborhoods; high-curvature regions get smaller ones. The post's figure reports the method beating both plain k-NN and an earlier adaptive k-NN on balanced accuracy across six datasets, with the largest gains at small training sizes (dataset 1, as transcribed from the figure: k-NN 0.531, adaptive 0.687, kK-NN 0.886 balanced accuracy; figure values CITED from the post's image).
